content: Controversy exists regarding whether long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) are essential nutrients for preterm infants. This is because preterm infants may lack the ability to synthesize sufficient amounts of LCPUFAs to meet the developmental needs of their brain and retina. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and potential benefits of supplementing formula milk with LCPUFAs for preterm infants, with a focus on their effects on visual function, neurodevelopment, and physical growth. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, up to February 28, 2016. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov in April 2016. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized trials that compared LCPUFA-supplemented formula with standard formula in enterally-fed preterm infants, specifically assessing outcomes related to visual development, neurodevelopment, and physical growth. Trials that only reported biochemical outcomes were excluded. Seventeen trials involving a total of 2,260 preterm infants were included in the review. The median gestational age of the infants was 30 weeks, and the median birth weight was 1,300 grams. The median concentration of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) in the supplemented formulas was 0.33% (ranging from 0.15% to 1%), while the median concentration of arachidonic acid (AA) was 0.37% (ranging from 0.02% to 0.84%). The risk of bias varied across the included studies, with 10 trials demonstrating a low risk of bias in most domains. Visual Acuity: Visual acuity was assessed in the first year of life using Teller or Lea acuity cards in eight studies, visual evoked potential (VEP) in six studies, and electroretinogram (ERG) in two studies. Most studies did not find significant differences in visual acuity between infants receiving LCPUFA-supplemented formula and those receiving standard formula. Due to differences in data presentation and assessment methods, meta-analysis was not feasible. A GRADE analysis indicated that the overall quality of evidence for this outcome was low. Neurodevelopment: Three out of seven studies reported some benefits of LCPUFA supplementation on neurodevelopment at various postnatal ages. However, a meta-analysis of four studies that evaluated the Bayley Scales of Infant Development at 12 months (364 infants) showed no significant effect of supplementation on the Mental Development Index (MDI) (mean difference [MD] 0.96, 95% confidence interval [CI] −1.42 to 3.34; P = 0.43; I² = 71%) or the Psychomotor Development Index (PDI) (MD 0.23, 95% CI −2.77 to 3.22; P = 0.88; I² = 81%). Similarly, three studies at 18 months (494 infants) found no significant effect of LCPUFA supplementation on neurodevelopment (MDI: MD 2.40, 95% CI −0.33 to 5.12; P = 0.08; I² = 0%; PDI: MD 0.74, 95% CI −1.90 to 3.37; P = 0.58; I² = 54%). A GRADE analysis indicated that the overall quality of evidence for these outcomes was low. Physical Growth: Four out of 15 studies reported benefits of LCPUFA supplementation on growth at different postmenstrual ages, while two studies suggested that supplemented infants grew less well. One trial reported mild reductions in length and weight z-scores at 18 months. A meta-analysis of five studies (297 infants) showed increased weight (MD 0.21, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.33; P = 0.001; I² = 69%) and length (MD 0.47, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.94; P = 0.05; I² = 0%) at two months post-term in supplemented infants. However, a meta-analysis of four studies at a corrected age of 12 months (271 infants) showed no significant effect of supplementation on weight (MD −0.10, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.12; P = 0.34; I² = 65%), length (MD 0.25, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.84; P = 0.40; I² = 71%), or head circumference (MD −0.15, 95% CI −0.53 to 0.23; P = 0.45; I² = 0%). Similarly, no significant effects on weight, length, or head circumference were observed in a meta-analysis of two studies (396 infants) at 18 months (weight: MD −0.14, 95% CI −0.39 to 0.10; P = 0.26; I² = 66%; length: MD −0.28, 95% CI −0.91 to 0.35; P = 0.38; I² = 90%; head circumference: MD −0.18, 95% CI −0.53 to 0.18; P = 0.32; I² = 0%). A GRADE analysis indicated that the overall quality of evidence for growth outcomes was low. Conclusions: The infants included in the trials were relatively mature and healthy preterm infants. There was significant variability in the assessment schedules, methodologies, doses, sources of supplementation, and fatty acid composition of the control formulas across the studies. When pooling the results, no clear long-term benefits or harms were observed for preterm infants receiving LCPUFA-supplemented formula.
